catalog_quote: [Bodt 2024 p.156, sec. 4.2] Whereas in Khispi and Duhumbi the meter in most words consists of a stressed syllable followed by one or more unstressed syllables, in the Sartang and Sherdukpen varieties an unstressed syllable is followed by a stressed syllable, in other words, the Khispi and Duhumbi rhythm is trochaic, that of the Sartang and Sherdukpen varieties iambic. [p.170-171, sec. 4.4.1] The Sartang and Sherdukpen varieties, on the other hand, obtained iambic rhythm through language contact, stressing the second syllable of a word, which, in the case of prefixed words, is always the root and not the prefix. Because of the lack of stress on the prefix, the prefix loses its vowel, either by replacement with a shwa or by complete elision. [p.301, sec. 50c] The short vowel rhymes are conditioned by a lack of stress on these suffixes. [Jacquesson 2018 p.28, sec. 2.4.4] More nouns are 2-syllable, and in this case, we either have a real compound and each syllable is pronounced, or a strong accent on the last syllable which tends to reduce the first vowel to a short copy of the next vowel (see 1.5.2) [p.30, sec. 2.5.2] The stress or accent is then on the second syllable (the verb root), and the first syllable (the negative prefix) is shortened to the point of having only a reduced vowel (biling-) or no vowel (bling-).
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Sherdukpen (both Rupa and Shergaon) has iambic word rhythm: in the typical (prefix+)root word the first syllable is unstressed, short and often reduced to schwa or zero, and stress falls on the second syllable, which is the root; grammatical suffixes are unstressed (Bodt p.300: short suffix rhymes 'conditioned by a lack of stress on these suffixes'). Jacquesson (2015/2018, Rupa) states the same first-hand: non-compound disyllabic nouns carry 'a strong accent on the last syllable' with reduction of the first vowel, and in negated verbs 'the stress or accent is then on the second syllable (the verb root)'. Net: stress on the root = second/last syllable of the prosodic stem; could also be filed as fixed: second syllable/final-of-stem (iambic).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Jacquesson: true compounds keep both syllables full (each syllable pronounced) rather than showing the reduced-first-syllable iambic pattern; s+stop clusters (spu 'cow', stu 'horse') are monosyllables, never restored as CvCV; degree of first-vowel reduction varies by speaker and speech rate (full vowel or echo vowel in slow/elicited speech, Bodt p.171 likewise). Bodt notes a few items retaining a full-vowel prefix, suggesting the trochaic>iambic shift is recent and uneven. Tone: Jacquesson says tones survive only in three small villages and are lost in Rupa; Boro 2024 posits H1/H2/L tones for Rupa; Bodt describes a glottal-constricted rising-pitch vowel series rather than tone.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (prefix+root+suffix word; elicited citation forms and connected speech both discussed). Bodt's statement is a generalisation over all Sartang and Sherdukpen varieties from his own fieldwork on Rupa and Shergaon; Jacquesson's statements are specific to Rupa (Thong clans) Sherdukpen.
new_statements.identity_note: Bodt 2024's stress statement is framed for 'the Sartang and Sherdukpen varieties' jointly (his Sherdukpen data = Rupa and Shergaon, both under sher1257; Sartang is a separate Glottolog language). Jacquesson 2015/2018 describes Rupa Sherdukpen as spoken by the Thong clans; Boro 2024 also Rupa; Dondrup 1988 reportedly Shergaon. Wikipedia/Glottolog dialects: Rupa (Tukpen) and Shergaon.

tone_statements.citation: Bodt, Timotheus Adrianus. 2019. The Duhumbi perspective on Proto-Western Kho-Bwa rhymes. Die Sprache 52(2): 141-176. Wiesbaden: Harrassowitz. (Open accepted manuscript: SOAS Research Online eprint 34574, 31 pp.)
tone_statements.quote: The short, glottal constricted, creaky voiced and rising pitch open vowels in the contemporary Western Kho-Bwa varieties are transcribed with a superscript glottal stop following the vowel [vˀ], although they would more accurately be transcribed as [v̰́ˀ]. These short vowels contrast with their long, breathy voiced, level pitch counterparts, which are represented in the Sartang and Sherdukpen varieties with [vː] although they would more accurately be transcribed as [v̤̄ː ~ v̄ːʱ].
tone_statements.locator: accepted manuscript p. 3, sec. 1 'Introduction' (notational conventions paragraph); journal pagination 141-176 not visible in the MS

sources.citation: Boro, Hirak Jyoti Lahari. 2024. A preliminary study of Sherdukpen phonology. Himalayan Linguistics 23(2) (Languages and Peoples of the Eastern Himalayan Region): 35-52. doi:10.5070/H923258183
sources.note: Silent on word stress/accent (no occurrence of 'stress' or 'accent'). Describes 23 consonants, vowels, diphthongs, syllable types, and posits three tones (H1 high short/glottal-constricted, H2 high long, L low) for Rupa from Praat data, while the conclusion says 'The Shergaon variety has tones, whereas, the Rupa variety has no tones' (internally inconsistent).

tone.quote: Three prominent tones have emerged from the analysis … They are H1, H2 and L. The H1 tone is the high tone having no constriction. The H2 is also a high tone but it has a glottal constriction. And the last tone L is clearly the low tone. … Tone 1 (High and short) (H1) ha ‘food’ kho ‘cane stick’ li ‘bow’ Tone 2 (High and long) (H2) kho ‘tax’ Tone 3 (Low) (L) ha ‘blood’ kho ‘water’ li ‘sacred stone’ … The dialect that I am discussing here is the Rupa dialect. … The Shergaon variety has tones, whereas, the Rupa variety has no tones.
tone.locator: p.47, sec. 4 'Tones' with Table 30 and p.51, sec. 6 'Conclusion'
tone.says: Unresolved: one study posits three tones (H1, H2, L) for Rupa yet concludes Rupa has no tones and Shergaon has; other descriptions treat the same contrast as checked/creaky short vs long vowels.

sources.note: No tonal analysis and the word 'tone' is not applied to Kho-Bwa; but the notational conventions state first-hand that the contemporary Western Kho-Bwa varieties, Sartang and Sherdukpen included, contrast short, glottal-constricted, creaky-voiced, rising-pitch open vowels [vˀ] with long, breathy-voiced, level-pitch vowels [vː] - i.e. the contrast Boro 2024 labels H2 vs L is treated here as a glottalisation/phonation-plus-pitch register contrast on open syllables, not as lexical tone. Elsewhere the paper discusses unstressed suffixes and prefix reduction (stress), not tone.
